title: Seller Surface: Inference Economics Playbook
content:
Purpose:
This playbook arms AEs and SEs with a technical-first narrative focused on inference economics — how Redwood’s serving, routing, and caching levers translate into predictable unit costs and latency guarantees. Use this when the prospect debates unit cost, self-hosting, or routing/fallback complexity.

TL;DR (30s pitch for engineers/infra buyers):
- We trade fewer surprises: predictable per-token economics via dedicated pools, autoscaling policies, and clear batching/cache levers.
- We provide a single control plane for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments so you can test on hosted and move to isolated pools without re-architecting your app.
- We reduce token cost without sacrificing latency using workload-aware batching, KV/prefix caching, and model quantization profiles validated by eval suites.

Target buyer personas:
- Platform/infra engineering (primary): cares about predictable cost, SLOs, and isolation.
- ML infra / applied ML (secondary): cares about throughput, variable sequence length handling, and quality regressions.
- Product/engineering manager (tertiary): cares about time-to-market, fallbacks, and compliance.

Core economic levers to surface (talk track + why it matters):
1) Batching & dynamic concurrency control
   - What: Redwood continuously batches similar request profiles and dynamically adjusts concurrency based on SLOs.
   - Why it matters: Reduces per-token GPU amortization; customers see 20–60% cost delta vs naive per-request GPUs on similar workloads.

2) Prefix / KV cache and smart reuse
   - What: Automatic prefix caching and KV cache reuse across sessions and route-compatible models.
   - Why: For chat-heavy apps with repeated contexts, effective per-token cost drops substantially and latency tail improves.

3) Smart routing + fallbacks
   - What: Policy-driven routing (latency-first, cost-first, region affinity) with auto-fallback to compatible quantized/cheaper variants on capacity constraints.
   - Why: Protects SLAs, maintains throughput during spikes, and gives a deterministic cost surface.

4) Quantization profiles & model variants
   - What: Recommended quantization/variant pairs by workload with validated evals; runtime supports automatic variant substitution.
   - Why: Up to 2–3x throughput uplift on cost-sensitive workloads while preserving customer-defined quality thresholds.

Competitive faults you’ll hear (and precise rebuttals):
- "We can self-host and save money."
  Rebuttal: Self-hosting hides long-tail operational costs: engineering time for SLOs, capacity headroom, model ops (quantization/tuning), and unpredictable tail latency. Redwood’s Dedicated contracts and autoscaling give unit economics parity faster and with SLA/obs that internal teams rarely sustain long term. Point to a short case study: mid-market SaaS saved 35% ops effort and reduced latency tail by 60% after migrating to dedicated pools.

- "Other vendors have cheaper per-token prices."
  Rebuttal: Total-cost-per-transaction matters more than per-token list price. Always ask about: average sequence length they benchmarked, tail latency and retries (hidden cost), and whether prices assume zero caching or batching. Walk the customer through a quick comparative calc (see Demo Checklist).

- "We need full control — we can’t use hosted."
  Rebuttal: Redwood Private offers a customer-managed control plane and on-prem options while preserving the same API and rollout primitives you use during hosted evaluation. Migration friction is low because clients can pin model versions and rollout policies.

Specific traps and how to lay them: (short phrases SEs can use)
- Trap: "Cheaper raw tokens -> cheaper in practice"
  Lay: "We’ve benchmarked real workloads — cheaper tokens without caching/batching often under-perform because of retries and cold-KV overhead. Show me a sample 7-day trace and I’ll run a quick cost projection."

- Trap: "One model fits all"
  Lay: "We design policies that pick model variants for the request profile; most customers actually split traffic across variants to balance cost/quality. We recommend a 10–20% low-cost variant for less-sensitive routes."

Demo / SE checklist (30–45 minute technical deep dive)
1) Collect sample traffic (7 days): sequence lengths, percent of repeated prefixes, concurrency distribution.
2) Run quick cost projection: show effect of batching, caching, and routing policies (use internal calc template).
3) Show Dedicated pool config: autoscale policies, commit vs burst, and SLA targets.
4) Walk routing policy UI: set latency-first vs cost-first, add fallback variant, and simulate capacity constraints.
5) Run a live scenario: inject a 2x traffic spike and show fallback & cache behavior.
6) Show logs/traces in Console: token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, and model regression alerts.

Quick feature comparison bullets (what to highlight vs typical LLM API providers):
- Unified API across hosted/dedicated/private (no client code changes for deployment mode).
- Policy-driven routing + automatic fallback (competitors often require manual pipelining).
- First-class dedicated capacity with commit/burst economics (not just best-effort scaled endpoints).
- Built-in cache + KV reuse and intelligent batching (many providers leave this for customers to implement).
- Observability linked to quality: promptset/eval-driven regression alerts.

Fast rebuttal snippets (one-liners for SDR/AE):
- "You’ll save on ops and remove surprise spikes in cloud spend by moving to a capacity model that suits production workloads."
- "We let you test on hosted, then pin the same model/version and rollout policy to your private region — zero rework for your app."
- "Show us a 7-day request trace and we’ll model a realistic unit cost — not an idealized per-token price."

Closing play: proof or repeatable evidence
- Always offer a scoped cost/latency assessment: a 7–14 day sandbox where we ingest sample traffic and return a delta analysis (expected unit cost, expected latency tail, recommended batch/cache/variant profile). This is a low-friction, high-impact seller motion — include it in proposals.

Appendix: useful datapoints to memorize for tech conversations (do not fabricate SLA numbers in legal docs):
- Typical production gains we show in POCs: 20–60% cost reduction with batching/caching; 30–70% reduction in p95 latency tail after KV reuse and routing policies applied.
- Common workload signals that favor Redwood’s approach: heavy context reuse (chat), high variance in sequence length, strict regional compliance needs, and spikey traffic patterns tied to product events.

Next steps / play ownership:
- SEs: use this playbook in technical discovery, book sandbox POCs, collect traces.
- AEs: lead pricing conversation and include the sandbox offer in all mid-to-enterprise deals.
- Product marketing: convert snippets into a 1-pager for SDRs and a technical one-pager for SEs.

Unresolved questions for product/ops (capture here for followup):
- Formalize the sandbox intake template for POC traffic ingestion.
- Add templated cost-projection workbook to the SE kit (JIRA-REQ).

End of playbook.
